doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: High school bebop players and Detroit's auto-industry economy
summary: Older students like Charles McPherson, Lonnie Hillyer and Roy Brooks played bebop in the boiler room; reading requirements; Detroit's prosperity.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Lonnie Hillyer, Roy Brooks and those guys was in high school — they was like two years ahead of me. But every — like 7:30 in the morning they would be playing in the boiler room. This was back in the 50s. Because jazz wasn’t allowed to be played in the band room because the band director was nervous. He couldn’t stand to hear Charlie Parker’s work. “Cherokee” and “Donna Lee” and all that stuff. And these guys was playing the carbon copy of the record you know.
They were learning by ear, is that right?

They could read you see. There was always, at that particular time, it was required to read. Reading marches, classical stuff, and everybody was required to take private lessons then. I’m talking about the 40s and 50s. In other words in order to get into the band, there was a B band, an A band, you’d have a private teacher. That was a requirement. So then when you joined the band they would teach you, you could play these tunes. But there was no thing about learning to play the instrument you know. It was learning the music, not the instrument. The instrument, it was understood that you could play and you could read. So playing in the band is about interpretation, learning to interpret. Because we was playing music from Italy, Germany, all over you know. A wide repertoire of music you know, very good educational system because they introduced you to different cultures and whatnot. So in terms of — these guys were playing music and they would write out different — they could write. We learned how to write. Because they had studied with the great Barry Harris. You know. And they had older musicians that was — this was in Detroit — they had older musicians that were working in Detroit and they would go to New York to record for Blue Note or Columbia or wherever it would be, or Riverside or Impulse, and then they’d come back to Detroit and work because of the auto industry, the economy was so big here. know. The people was making money and people was working you know. People buying homes and forming businesses and creating businesses. So the infrastructure and the environment was very ludicrous [lucrative?] — actually prolific back in those days you know. People used to come in from the south and as far as Poland to come and work in the factory. People like Berry Gordy. He was working in the factory and he started Motown. A lot of businesses started as a byproduct of the auto industry.
